\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Corticolous Lichens as Bioindicators of Air Quality along an
Urban--Rural Gradient}
\author{E.~Falkenrath and T.~Okafor}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Corticolous lichens respond sensitively to atmospheric pollution and are
inexpensive to census. We surveyed the trunks of 240 street and park
trees along a 60~km urban--rural gradient and recorded the frequency of
five indicator species, including \textit{Xanthoria parietina} and
\textit{Physcia adscendens}. Species richness doubled from the city
centre to the rural endpoint, while the nitrophilous
\textit{Xanthoria parietina} showed the opposite trend.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Lichens lack a cuticle and absorb water and solutes directly from the
atmosphere, which makes them effective accumulators of airborne
pollutants. The classic indicator \textit{Hypogymnia physodes} is
tolerant of moderate sulphur deposition, whereas
\textit{Evernia prunastri} is among the first species to disappear from
polluted urban cores. Community approaches therefore complement
instrumental monitoring at a fraction of the cost.

\section{Field Methods}
At each of 24 sites we censused ten mature trees, recording the presence
and cover of every macrolichen on the lower two metres of the trunk.
\textit{Parmelia sulcata} was recorded separately from the morphologically
similar \textit{Parmelia saxatilis} using the isidium and soralium
characters of the upper cortex. Nomenclature follows the standard
checklist for the region.

\section{Results}
\textit{Xanthoria parietina} occurred at every urban site but declined
beyond 40~km from the centre, consistent with its nitrophilous
ecology. \textit{Physcia adscendens} showed a similar but weaker
pattern. In contrast, \textit{Evernia prunastri} appeared only beyond
25~km, and \textit{Hypogymnia physodes} reached peak cover at the rural
endpoint. \textit{Parmelia sulcata} was ubiquitous and uninformative as
an indicator.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Frequency of indicator species along the gradient (percent of sites).}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\hline
Species & Urban & Intermediate & Rural \\
\hline
\textit{Xanthoria parietina} & 100 & 75 & 38 \\
\textit{Physcia adscendens} & 88 & 62 & 25 \\
\textit{Parmelia sulcata} & 100 & 100 & 100 \\
\textit{Hypogymnia physodes} & 12 & 50 & 88 \\
\textit{Evernia prunastri} & 0 & 38 & 75 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Discussion}
The turnover from \textit{Xanthoria parietina}-dominated urban
communities to \textit{Hypogymnia physodes}-rich rural assemblages
mirrors the pollution gradient inferred from instrumental stations,
supporting lichen censusing as a low-cost complement to air-quality
monitoring.

\end{document}
